Log in here » KONOTOPIE, Poland (AP) — An enormous statue of the Virgin Mary that is believed to be Europe’s tallest was inaugurated on Saturday in a small Polish village, in the presence of legendary anti-communist leader Lech Walesa. Hundreds of people took part in the consecration of the monument, which towers 55.6 meters (182 feet) over Konotopie in central Poland, the home of fewer than 150 people. While helicopters scattered miniature red roses over the crowd, priests in white robes celebrated Mass and the popular Mazowsze folk ensemble sang and danced to traditional Polish music. People walk inside an enormous statue of the Virgin Mary that is believed to be Europe's tallest during the inauguration in the village Konotopie, Poland, Saturday, Aug. 15, 2026. (AP Photo/Claudia Ciobanu) The Polish statue is taller — if less dramatically located — than the Christ the Redeemer statue in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, which measures some 38 meters (125 feet) including its pedestal. Its height includes a crown-shaped 15-meter (49-foot) pedestal. It also surpasses another recent large-scale religious monument in Poland, the Christ the King statue in the western town of Swiebodzin, which was unveiled in 2010 and — complete with the mound it stands on — rises some 52 meters (170 feet) above the ground. There is a taller statue of the Virgin Mary in the Philippines, which measures some 98 meters (322 feet). But the new one in Poland is believed to be the largest of its kind in Europe. An anti-communist legend celebrates Catholic Poland Walesa, who won the Nobel Peace Prize for his leadership of the Polish anti-communist resistance as the head of the Solidarity trade union, and was later Polish president, had a front row seat during the inauguration ceremony. “This is the end of my path,” the 82-year-old Walesa told the AP, suggesting that the causes he has long championed, including democracy and Catholic faith, are now completed. “I started with the Virgin Mary and I end with the Virgin Mary.” During his Solidarity days, Walesa famously wore a Black Madonna pin and has often credited his faith in God with giving him the strength to fight against communism. The vast majority of Poles identify as Catholic, and the Catholic church played a powerful role in public life after the fall of communism in 1989, benefiting from the prestige it earned through its support for the anti-communist opposition. The country is the homeland of St. John Paul II, who reigned as pope from 1978 until his death in 2005. A huge statue of him — but much smaller than the one of Mary — was unveiled over a decade ago in the city of Czestochowa. The influence of religion in public life has gradually declined in recent years, particularly among younger people and in urban areas. However, the Catholic church remains influential, especially in rural communities and among older generations. “I cannot help but notice the weakening of the institution of the church, a withdrawal of specific social categories from Catholicism, and this hurts me,” Bishop Wiesław Mering, a Polish Roman Catholic prelate who attended the ceremony, told the AP. “The history of Christianity has ups and downs but this place is a reminder that Mary won’t give up on Poland,” the bishop said. Local millionaires financed massive statue to give thanks to God The statue was commissioned by local millionaires Roman and Grażyna Karkosik. The couple live in a small palace a few kilometers (miles) from Konotopie. Roman Karkosik, an entrepreneur whose ventures included plastic-bottle manufacturing in the 1990s, amassed a fortune through investments on the Warsaw Stock Exchange to became one of Poland’s wealthiest individuals. Sign up for Sunday Passages The couple have said the monument is an expression of their gratitude to God. “The statue will be for all people,” Grażyna Karkosik told AP. “Each of us coming to see it will think more deeply about their own lives, not only about God.” Local authorities hope the monument will become both a major pilgrimage site and a tourist destination. The statue features a viewing platform built inside its pedestal. ___ Associated Press religion coverage receives support through the AP’s collaboration with The Conversation US, with funding from Lilly Endowment Inc. November 9, 2026 in Operations People and Skills Three steps to reduce employee turnover through better facility hygiene. Employee retention tends to fly under the radar at manufacturing facilities around the world, including those within Canada, largely because it’s difficult to measure and is often seen as a task of the HR department. “The hard measurable targets you have in a plant are production, efficiency and waste,” says Joe Merker, Key Account Manager for the Tork brand for the industrial sector. “Everybody is on the pulse of those things.” But employee retention? Not so much. Even when employers do measure turnover costs, Merker says, they often calculate only the direct expenses associated with recruitment – things like job postings, interview time and recruitment fees. But those are just the tip of the iceberg. The cost of losing a good employee extends well beyond training and onboarding a new hire; it also includes the operational drag that comes when valuable skills, experience and institutional knowledge walk out the door. All things considered, the average cost of turnover per employee sits at $30,680 , according to a 2025 survey conducted by Express Employment Professionals of more than 500 Canadian hiring decision-makers. And with 67 per cent of manufacturers dealing with headcount reductions, retention becomes even more critical: employers need to hold on to experienced workers while staying competitive for talent as the labour market shifts. The opportunity: tackling turnover within a facility When it comes to retention, Merker says, a manufacturing facility itself – from hygiene stations to break rooms and washrooms – can be a recruitment and retention tool, and one that’s often overlooked by many manufacturers. Facilities aren’t just overhead, Merker argues – they’re operational systems that directly impact productivity and morale on the plant floor. “If people feel they’re working in unorganized or unsanitary conditions, or they don’t have easy access to proper cleaning supplies, they start to feel, in spite of what you say, that you don’t really care about them,” he says. “And that creates an us-versus-them mentality.” To ensure a facility works in your favour when it comes to retaining valuable employees, Merker urges employers to understand the pain points in an employee’s workday, even if that means having “hard, honest conversations with them.” Regular hygiene audits of washrooms, break rooms and the plant floor can then confirm what employees are telling you, and show where to act first. Here’s a three-step plan to get started: Step 1: Keep employee comfort in mind Photo courtesy of Tork. Employee areas play an important role in how people experience a facility day to day. Clean, well-stocked washrooms and inviting break rooms signal that comfort, health and dignity are part of the workplace culture – not afterthoughts. When handwashing stations and shared spaces are consistently supplied with personal hygiene essentials, they support a workplace culture where handwashing and hygiene are treated as everyday priorities rather than an extra effort. “When you ask people to use a consistently unstocked washroom or an uninviting break room, you’re telling them that leadership simply doesn’t prioritize their basic health and comfort,” Merker says. “And if someone’s stomach is a little upset and the restrooms on the plant floor aren’t as sanitary as they need to be, or consistently out of toilet paper, soap or paper towels, they may just decide to take a sick day.” That matters not only for morale, but also for absenteeism: facilities that make good hygiene easy also help reduce the spread of illness, which keeps more people healthy and on the job. This can directly impact a facility’s ability to hold on to good employees. According to professional hygiene brand Tork and its Global Insights Survey, seventeen per cent of respondents said they left a job because of poor restroom conditions, and one in four people spent less time at their workplace due to poor restrooms. [1] Even if the facility itself is clean, the employee experience suffers when essential items are not easy to access where and when they are needed. “If people have to work in less-than-ideal conditions, they will find other options down the road,” Merker says. Making hygiene and cleaning products consistently available – and placing them close to the point of use – also shows staff that their comfort and time are being considered, while helping reduce unnecessary motion waste throughout the facility. Step 2: Show employees you value their time Small workflow frustrations can add up quickly on the plant floor, especially when employees must leave their workstations to find the supplies they need. And yet, according to the Tork brand’s research , 44 per cent of workers report being interrupted up to 20 times during a workday because they have to find rags or dispose of wipes and other cleaning tools on the plant floor. “If you’re looking at your facility’s workflow, why would you want somebody to stop their task, turn off their machine and walk 100 feet to get a cleaning cloth?” Merker asks. “Every step is a second lost.” Placing dispensers for wipers and cleaning materials throughout your facility where they’re needed shows employees you’re truly trying to make it easy for them to do their jobs – and may even boost productivity in the process. If that’s not reason enough to place cleaning products at key places on the machine line and on the plant floor, consider how it might help the bottom line in the long run. “Our research indicates 74 per cent of workers grab more wipers or cloths than they really need in order to save themselves a walk to the dispenser,” Merker says. “That results in higher costs for the employer.” That’s where a consultative approach can help connect facility hygiene to broader operational priorities, Merker advises. Tork’s partnership approach starts with understanding how hygiene practices affect the facility as a whole, from employee experience to workflow, maintenance and productivity. Simple changes, such as installing high-capacity dispensers, can help ensure supplies are protected, accessible and available when employees need them. Step 3: Match the tool to the task Placing supplies strategically is just the beginning, Merker says. The correct supplies must always be stocked for the task at hand. And using ineffective wipers, such as rags and rental towels, can waste employees’ time and, in some cases, be harmful to their health or damage machinery. “Rags and rental towels can retain small amounts of heavy metals, residual chemicals and harmful bacteria which can pose a health risk to employees and a threat to sensitive manufacturing equipment, even after they are laundered,” Merker says. In addition, that rag pile can increase the risk of a slip and fall injury to your employees. “If a rag falls on an epoxy floor and someone steps on it, it’s like wearing a roller skate.” In contrast, purpose-made wipers designed for one-time use that are placed where they’re most needed reduce wasted motion and the risk of contamination for employees, products and equipment. And, because they’re fabricated with engineered fibres that distribute liquids more efficiently, they help employees get the job done faster. “They can reduce solvent consumption by up to 40 per cent and reduce cleaning time by up to 35 per cent,” Merker explains, helping employees spend less of the workday on repetitive tasks and more time meeting productivity goals. The bottom line Ultimately, Merker says, seemingly small things like conducting regular hygiene audits and providing the right supplies and equipment in washrooms, break rooms and on the plant floor send a powerful message to employees, showing them that their comfort, health and ability to do their jobs well are being supported. “Employers tell me their people are their most important assets,” Merker says. “If you’re able to give people the tools they need to do their jobs efficiently in a comfortable and clean work environment, you can differentiate yourself as an employer who really cares about your people,” Merker says. Through its specialized, complimentary assessment program known as Tork Workflow , Tork conducts 60-minute audits of client facilities to determine operational pain points around maintenance, workstation and professional hygiene practices. Visit Tork Global for more information. [1] Tork Insight Survey 2025, conducted in US, UK, Germany, France, Mexico, Canada, Australia, Spain, Sweden, Netherlands and Poland among 11,500 people from the general public and 1,000 cleaning staff. Created by Amplify Content Studio , in partnership with Tork, an Essity brand, and Plant. Twelve questions to ask about hygiene and maintenance in your facility A manufacturing facility that’s not optimized for hygiene can consume valuable time, reduce output and lower employee satisfaction and morale. Looking for ways to improve? Ask the following questions: 1. Are there touchless paper towel and soap dispensers in the washrooms that function smoothly and don’t jam? 2. Are washrooms and break rooms always well-stocked with napkins, paper towels, toilet paper, soap and other hygiene products? 3. Are those items accessible to all employees? Can people with limited reach or hand strength access them? 4. Is toilet paper housed in protected, enclosed high-capacity dispensers to prevent loose rolls on toilet backs? 5. Does every bathroom stall have working door locks and latches and privacy screens at urinals? 6. Are there disposal bins for personal products in every stall? 7. How clean are washrooms and break rooms? Is the air fresh? Are floors clean and waste bins of an adequate size? Are sinks free of standing water and debris? 8. Are sanitizing wipes or colour-coded cloths conveniently placed near food prep areas? 9. Are centre-feed or counter towels placed right next to sinks and appliances in break rooms for ease of use? 10. How far do employees have to walk to get cleaning supplies on the plant floor? 11. Are purpose-made wipers directly designed for the task at hand provided? 12. Is there a hygiene transparency indicator, such as a cleaning log or digital tracking system, visible for employees to see? Photograph: Jack Hill/PA Brexit Burnham: I won’t listen to ex-Tory PMs who left UK with ‘bad Brexit deal’ PM says closer ties with EU will lower cost of living, with ‘brainstorming’ sessions being mooted to discuss shape of future relationship UK politics live – latest updates Jessica Elgot Deputy political editor Mon 23 Nov 2026 11.40 EST Last modified on Mon 23 Nov 2026 11.41 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Andy Burnham has criticised former prime ministers for being “stuck in the past” amid warnings over re-opening the Brexit debate, with informal talks now set to take place with Brussels about how the UK could forge even closer ties with the EU. After a major summit between UK and EU leaders on Friday when trade and youth mobility deals were struck, Brussels signalled a willingness to begin “brainstorming” sessions with UK officials and ministers about the shape of the future relationship, including options of a Swiss-style deal with close sectoral alignment, a single market and customs union deal or a path for Britain to rejoin the EU as a full member. Burnham said there would now be discussions in the run-up to the next summit, which is expected to result in a deal brokered on UK participation in the EU’s internal electricity market, and political dialogue on a longer-term, deeper relationship. Officials in both the EU and UK have signalled they would like to see those discussions with Brussels run in parallel to the “national debate” that Burnham has said he wishes to have with the UK public about what the closer future relationship might look like. Burnham said the food and drink deal signed with the EU on Friday would directly cut costs for shoppers and dismissed the advice of former prime ministers, including Rishi Sunak, David Cameron and Theresa May who have said he should not reignite the Brexit debate. “I’m not sure they’re the people I’ll be listening to here because they left Britain with a bad Brexit deal,” he said. “They’re stuck in the past because they can’t face up to the bad deal that they did. “I’m not a prime minister that’s going to be stuck in the past. I want to lead Britain forward to a more hopeful future, get the economy growing again, get cost of living down for people, lower energy bills. “All of these things can be achieved by a more positive, constructive relationship with the European Union . I believe it will be better for Britain to take this path, and I won’t be listening to those voices who put us here in the first place.” The legal text of the deal, expected in the coming days, is also likely to contain a clause which would penalise the UK if it reneged on the deal in order to pay the costs of reinstating customs infrastructure – which opposition parties have dubbed a “Farage clause” should the Reform UK leader win the next election and reverse the deal. Burnham, who will lay legislation next week to implement the food and drink deal, said that major supermarkets had confirmed it would “lift the pressure off the weekly shop”. Speaking at a Morrison’s distribution centre, he said: “They’ve just shown me a stack of paperwork which they have to fill in when they export from here to their store in Gibraltar. “If you remove that paperwork, that red tape, you can lower the cost, and they say it will lower the pressure on the weekly shop.” Jukka Salovaara, the EU ambassador to the UK, told reporters on Monday that the agreements would have a direct impact on ordinary people. “The big beneficiaries are young people, businesses and farmers. Removing these barriers should lead to more trade on both sides and increased UK exports. “What is made in Great Britain will be good to go for the EU market. UK companies exporting to the EU will no longer have to pay the associated carbon charge. This is a major benefit for UK businesses.” Explore more on these topics Brexit Foreign policy European Union Andy Burnham Europe Labour Conservatives news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development
